newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem mired in worst crisis in years.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem mired in worst crisis in years.

text.p: The Argentine government, only four months before key midterm elections, is mired in its worst crisis in years as it struggles with social unrest and a snowballing scandal over links to an alleged mobster.

And just when it should be united, analysts say, the ruling Peronist party is split by divisions so bitter they are weakening the administration's ability to cope with criticism from the public, church and political opposition.
After being reelected with 50 percent of the vote two years ago, President Carlos Menem appears hard-pressed now to garner even double digit support in some polls.

"Menem is in a tremendously difficult situation," political analyst James Nielson said. "He is betting on having enough popular support in time for the elections in October and recovering political capital but there is no guarantee this will happen."
The protests and political scandal have enabled the centre-left Frepaso party to trim the Peronist lead to between two to five points in the campaign for congressional polls.
"This must be the worst crisis since 1991," when the government was plagued by a political crisis and economic tumult, historian and pollster Rosendo Fraga said.

Menem, however, downplays opposition, telling reporters on the weekend that the political climate has "never been better" and rejecting newspaper reports that he is set to jettison some cabinet members to polish the administration's image.
Television viewers have been fed a regular diet of vivid images from the interior of Argentina, with people blocking roads with burning tires to protest joblessness.

Some of these are victims of economic reforms Menem implemented after taking office in 1989 that, while eliminating decades of hyperinflation and generating strong economic growth, tossed thousands out of their jobs.
Unemployment nationwide is 17.3 percent but soars to as high as 40 percent in some of the areas where protests erupt.

In the capital last Friday, thousands of teachers and student supporters marched through the streets to a white tent outside Congress where state-sector teachers have been staging a hunger strike since April to demand higher salaries.

The president has managed to further infuriate Argentines with his dismissive style. Responding to complaints from Bishop Rafael Rey, head of the Catholic charity Caritas, who suggested it was a moral crime that Argentine children were dying of hunger, Menem said: "I have seen nothing in the Penal Code on this, unless it is a crime invented by Monsignor Rey."
The government has also found itself on the defensive in the case of a news photographer who was murdered at a beach resort last January.

A former policeman was arrested for the killing. But police say postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran, alleged by former Economy Ministry Domingo Cavallo to be a mafia boss, is their "only lead" as to who ordered the murder.

For two years, Yabran has been at the heart of allegations of corruption and money laundering in the government. The administration's denials that Yabran has any influence on it crumbled last week when Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan both admitted they got phone calls from him.
Menem denies he and Yabran are friends but that is contradicted by the president's ex-wife.
"The Yabran case is affecting it a lot," pollster Felipe Noguera said. "When a government has incidents that wear it out so strongly, it is difficult to recuperate."
